textContent.text: Daniel woke up to the sound of hooves pounding down the dirt road. He rubbed his eyes and peeked out his bedroom window into the dark midnight sky. A rider on a horse shot past, calling out words Daniel couldn't quite make out. One by one, lanterns came to life in the houses nearby. The townspeople opened their doors and leaned out, gazing into the night.
Daniel's stomach turned when his father pulled on his boots and hurried outside. Daniel pressed his face to the window glass, his mind racing with questions.
As the rider passed their gate a second time, Daniel finally caught the words.
"Awake!" the rider shouted. "Storm is coming! Tie down the wagons! Sound the alarm!"
Daniel relaxed his shoulders, let out a big sigh, and stepped outside to help prepare for the storm.

content.text: How does hearing the rider announce the storm change how Daniel is feeling?

choices.text: He goes from worried to calm.
He goes from angry to scared.

textContent.text: Lee kept glancing at the gym door, waiting. He checked the clock again, tapping his foot.
"You can go ahead," he told the girl behind him. She stepped forward and karate chopped the wooden board in two. The class clapped, and Lee tightened his belt. His eyes darted back to the door.
When the teacher looked at him, Lee shook his head. "I need some water first," he said.
He started toward his water bottle, but stopped when he heard the door open. Lee's mom rushed in, smiling and out of breath. "Never mind," Lee called to his teacher. "I'm ready now!"

textContent.text: Deep inside Grandpa's mountain castle, Linea sat beside the humming time machine. Its buttons blinked, and with a sudden buzz, the door slid open.
Grandpa stepped out with messy hair and a seashell in one hand.
"You should've seen that beach, Linea," he said softly. "Warm sand and a bright sky. It was the best morning ever."
He pressed the smooth shell into Linea's hand. She carefully placed it on the nearly full shelf of bottles, coins, and shells from other trips.
"Wow," Linea said. "We're running out of room for all your treasures."
Grandpa's eyes lit up. "Let's build another shelf! We can fill that one, too!"

textContent.text: Tony the Troll stared out at his brown, lifeless garden. All week, he had watered the flowers, sung to them, and even read them poems, but nothing worked.

As he lay awake that night wondering what to do, he spotted a soft light drifting through the air. A faint sound followed, like tiny bells. Tony crept to the window and peeked out. A small fairy with silver wings floated above his garden. She held out her tiny hand filled with magic dust, and began sprinkling it all over the ground. The fairy spun around and noticed Tony watching. She winked before disappearing into the night.
The next morning, Tony rushed outside and jumped for joy. His garden was full of tall, colorful flowers!

title.text: The Day the Butterflies Were Found

passage.text: Rosa milked the cow, the milk splashing against the metal bucket. Nearby, Papá fed the donkey.
"Buenos días," a voice said.
Rosa glanced up to see a man and woman standing in the barn doorway. Outsiders, Rosa decided. She knew almost everyone who lived around here. Besides, the pair wore city clothes.
"Buenos días," Papá answered, standing up straight. "Can I help you?"
"Yes, thank you," the woman smiled. "I'm Catalina, and this is Ken. We're trying to find a secret place."
"A secret place?"
The man held up a picture of some orange-and-black butterflies. "Have you seen these butterflies?"
Papá laughed. "No secret there," he said. "They pass through every November."

"Hundreds of them!" Rosa added, coming to stand next to Papá. "Some say the butterflies are the spirits of our dead loved ones." Rosa wasn't sure what she thought about that. Still, she loved it when the butterflies came.
"They're beautiful, aren't they?" Catalina said. "Every winter, they fly away from Canada and the United States. But no one knows where they end up. It's like they just disappear!"

"The scientist we work for thinks they all live together someplace, maybe right here in Mexico," Ken said. "But Dr. Urquhart has been searching for years, and he hasn't found their spot yet. We're hoping to crack this mystery."
"Wow," said Rosa.

Papá pointed. "All I know is they head up the mountain." Then he frowned, thinking. "My uncle once spoke about a lovely, special place he'd found while gathering mushrooms. He said it was so spectacular that he thought he was in a dream. I wonder..."

Then Rosa remembered something. "Once when Grandmother and I were picking blackberries, she said our loved ones might be sleeping nearby. I thought she was just trying to stop my chattering. But maybe..."
"Do you remember where you picked the blackberries?" Catalina asked.
Rosa nodded.
"Perhaps we can help after all," Papá said.

An hour later, Rosa, Papá, Catalina, and Ken hiked up the mountain to the blackberry patch. They searched the whole area but saw no butterflies. Then, Papá bent down. "I think these are the mushrooms my uncle liked."
They followed the mushrooms to where they grew thickest. And that's when Rosa spotted a butterfly. "There!" she cried.
"Let's follow it!" said Catalina. The group pressed forward, winding around rocks and sliding down hills.
Suddenly, there was a sound like gentle rain. Everyone stopped and looked up. "Far out," Ken whispered.
The trees looked orange.
Their branches were covered with thousands, maybe millions, of butterflies! Rosa felt like she was in a beautiful dream. She stared until her neck ached.
"January 2, 1975," she whispered, knowing she'd never forget it.

passage.text: Nathaniel ran a cloth over the books' rich covers. Dusting the family library was the job he liked best at the Brookes home.
Or maybe it made more sense to say that dusting the library was the job Nathaniel disliked least.
Back in 1604, Nathaniel had left his family's farm in search of adventure in London. Two years later, the only adventures he'd found were in these gold-lettered books.

Carefully, he pulled one down: Roanoke Colony. His heart pounded as he read about the English settlers who disappeared in Virginia. If only Nathaniel were rich! He'd use his money to sail to America and find the settlers' hidden messages. Maybe he'd even rescue them!
"Nathaniel!" William called. "You're needed in the kitchen!" Sighing, Nathaniel closed the book. No sailing for him. Just potatoes to peel.
Nathaniel found William at the work table, staring straight ahead. "King James is sending another group to America," William said. "Mr. Brookes signed on, and he wants me to join."
Nathaniel grabbed the back of a chair to steady himself.
William dropped his head into his hands. "They're not taking women, and I can't possibly leave Betsy."
"I'll go!" The words flew from Nathaniel's mouth. William could stay home with his wife, while Nathaniel set sail.
"Would you?" William looked up, but then he shook his head. "Ah, he'll never take you. You don't have the skills needed for such a long, important trip."
"What skills?" Nathaniel asked.
But William just stood up and sighed. It was time to return to work. "The men are meeting tonight to plan the expedition," he said, his voice weary. "Mr. Brookes wants you to take notes."
After dinner, Nathaniel returned to the library for the meeting. As the men talked, Nathaniel wrote what they listed: nails, hammers, needles, thread, salt, flour, rice...
Finally, Mr. Brookes announced, "I believe that's everything."
What? Were they planning to eat no vegetables or fruit in America? Swallowing, Nathaniel forced himself to speak. "Sir?"
"Yes?"
"Perhaps you'll need things for farming? Seeds, and—"

"Ah!" Mr. Brookes replied. "You're a farm boy, aren't you? Go ahead and list what we'll need." As Nathaniel wrote, he pretended he was joining the journey, and that he was in charge of the farming. His list grew and grew.
Later that night, Nathaniel was adding logs to the fireplace when William burst in, grinning. "What did you tell Mr. Brookes?"
Nathaniel looked up, startled. "Just—"
"He wants you to take my place on the expedition!" William exclaimed.
Nathaniel's mouth dropped open. "Me?"
"They need farmers! Will you still go?"
"Will I ever!"
William clapped Nathaniel on the back, then shook his hand. "I'll help you pack, settler."

passage.text: The Hester Street market was as lively as ever. But as Jacob and Papa set up their pushcart, Jacob felt slow and...blocky, somehow. Like he took up too much space. Through the dressmaker's shop window, he could see Ruth and her father cutting cloth. Ruth didn't look up.
Ruth was usually kind. Sometimes she and Jacob even shared treats from the pushcarts lining the street: pickles, hot potatoes, peppermint.
But yesterday, as Ruth had squeezed past them, Jacob heard her whisper, "These pushcarts! People should press themselves like fish to get in our door?"
Jacob had felt terrible.
"Papa," he said now, "Maybe we should set up somewhere else."

"Somewhere else?" Papa repeated, straightening the button boxes. He always said a button seller's cart should be neat as a button. "Rosen's Dressmakers is probably the best spot for a button pushcart in all of New York City!"
"But we're...in people's way."
Papa laughed. "Look around! We're all in each other's way. Good for business!"

Jacob sighed. He wished Papa had a real shop. He pictured a sign with gold letters: "Bornstein's Buttons, Established 1900." No, "Bornstein's Buttons, Established 1898." After all, Papa had been selling buttons for two years now.

"Bornstein?" said a voice. Jacob looked up. A carriage pulled by two horses had stopped in the street. Behind the driver sat a lady in a fine dress and ribboned hat. "Bornstein, the button seller?" she asked.
Papa nodded. The woman jumped down and showed them her boot. It was well-made, but a button was missing.
"Can you match these buttons?" she asked. "I already checked the uptown shops."
Papa bent to study the boot. Jacob felt the other sellers staring. Fancy people rarely came to Hester Street.
"An interesting design," Papa said, straightening.
The woman nodded, looking at the pushcart. "I didn't expect your...cart to be so small."
"Pushcarts hold more than they seem to," Papa said. "Jacob, the shell buttons are in the back row. Look for a robin inside a flower."
Jacob started at one end, Papa at the other. They opened boxes and boxes of buttons. Finally, Jacob opened a small white box, and ten robins—each inside a flower—stared up at him. "Papa!"
Papa and the woman bent their heads over the box. "That's it!" she exclaimed.
"Thirty cents," Papa smiled.
"That's all? The uptown shops..."
"Running a pushcart costs less than running a shop."
"Then I'll start buying all my buttons from you." The lady looked around. "Ooh, I didn't know there was a dressmaker here!"
Turning, Jacob saw Ruth in the doorway. She looked at Jacob in surprise as the new customer approached her.
Jacob smiled. He and Papa didn't need a shop. Their neat-as-a-button pushcart held far more than Jacob had known.

passage.text: "My insides feel funny," Mukta said.
"Mine, too," Padma whispered.
As the sisters left their family's farm, the chickens scratched in the tea-colored dirt. The sweet mangoes hung from the trees like green jewels. Everything was just as usual.
But there was nothing usual about the girls going to school.
"I hope our heads don't grow gigantic from everything we learn!" Mukta joked, trying not to think about the feeling in her stomach.
Padma laughed. "We'll need both hands to hold them up!"

Turning the corner, their laughter died out. A group of boys was heading into the boys' school, heads high. They looked so sure of themselves, like they knew exactly what to do. The sisters stood for a moment, watching the doors swing shut.
"Mukta," Padma said, "What if we don't know what to do?"
Mukta swallowed. "The teacher will show us. That's his job. It's not our fault there weren't girls' schools until now."
"Suppose they've changed their minds?" Padma worried, as they started walking again. "Suppose they've decided that learning really is just for boys, and girls should stay home—"
"It's 1848, not 1820!" Mukta waved her hand, but she was concerned, too. Perhaps the new school had already been shut down! Suddenly, she had to know. "Let's run," she said.
They ran fast, their sari dresses slapping their legs. When they reached the stone building, they stopped, breathing hard.
A lady in a pink sari waved from the door. Mukta and Padma glanced at each other. She was the teacher?
"Hello! I'm Mrs. Phule," said the lady. She looked at them carefully. "Is everything all right?"
"We were scared they changed their minds," Padma said. "About letting girls go to school."
Mukta's face burned, but Mrs. Phule just nodded. "Please, come inside. I want to show you something."

Shyly, the girls stepped inside the small room. The floor was swept clean, with small mats for the children to sit on. On each mat was a book. Mrs. Phule led them to a large map covering the back wall.

"I understand why you got scared. After all, most girls in India still can't go to school," Mrs. Phule said. Her dark eyes danced. "To solve this problem, I'm starting girls' schools all over the country. This map shows where the schools will be. When I look at it, I feel strong and hopeful."

Mukta studied the map for a long time. I will learn to read the names of these places, she thought, and that made her feel strong. She imagined cleverness rising in her, growing like the strongest mango tree. Growing in Padma too, and in so many other Indian girls—all starting school for the very first time.

Quentin nodded. It had been a week since Archie had seen his pony. "Maybe Mother will let you visit him."
"I asked. She said I have to stay in bed until I'm better."
Quentin looked out the window. The White House barn wasn't that far. He could see it from here. "You could ask Father," he suggested.

Archie scratched the red spots on his face. "I'm so tired of being sick," he said. "I wish there were medicine for measles."
"I know. Then there wouldn't be so many sick kids stuck in bed with nothing to do."
"And so many ponies bored in their barns."

He raced downstairs, out the back door, and into the barn, where he slipped a rope over Algonquin's head. Then he led the pony back to the White House. Once inside, he tiptoed down the back hallway, Algonquin clip-clopping behind him. At the elevator, Quentin sighed with relief. No one had seen!
"What in the world!" cried a voice. Quentin spun around, coming face-to-face with Mr. Reeder, a White House worker.
Only the truth would work. "Archie needs cheering up."
Mr. Reeder's face changed. "This is for your brother? Because he's sick?"
Quentin nodded, and Mr. Reeder grabbed Algonquin's rope. "Let's get in that elevator, horse."

At first, Algonquin refused to enter, no matter how hard they pulled. But then, he spotted his reflection in the elevator's mirror. Algonquin must have liked how he looked. He took a curious step forward...then another, and another. At last, he was inside.
"We've got this in the bag, son!" Mr. Reeder said, wiping his face and grinning.
Upstairs, they tiptoed and clip-clopped to Archie's door.

Then, everything happened at once. Quentin, Algonquin, and Mr. Reeder stormed into Archie's room. Archie yelled, and Algonquin slipped on the game pieces. Crash! Finally, Father charged in, booming, "What's happening?"
Quentin helped Algonquin up, while Mr. Reeder said, "Sir—"
But President Roosevelt held up a hand. His eyes were on Archie, who was smiling and hugging Algonquin. Father chuckled.
"Like Mother says, happiness is the best medicine!" Father winked at Quentin. "Just remember to return Algonquin to the barn. This house has enough pets already."

passage.text: Lila lifted the water jug from her head. She was finally home from her two-mile walk under the hot African sun. Mama handed her a cup of water that had been boiled and cooled. Lila drank deeply, then grabbed her basket. It was time to gather wood.
Wood and water, water and wood. These jobs took most of the day now.
It hadn't always been this way. The stream in their Kenyan village had once been full of water. Lila remembered the shadows of the tree branches dancing on its surface.
But the trees were gone now, too. A few years ago—1975, Lila remembered—some men had come and cut them down. Now, dead stumps lined the stream's dry banks.

Lost in thought, Lila almost bumped into Mama Anisa. The old woman smiled at her, then frowned at Lila's empty firewood basket. Mama Anisa held up her own basket. "When they took our trees, they took our firewood," she said.
Lila nodded. Mama Anisa must have been thinking about the old forest, too. "And our water as well," she added.
"They took our water?" Lila asked.
"In a way, yes," Mama Anisa replied. "Water needs shade, you see."
"So that's why our stream is dry?"
"Yes."

The two walked together, looking for wood. It took a long time, but at last their baskets were filled. They headed home on the dirt track, their feet aching as usual. A shiny black car bumped past them, and Mama Anisa sighed. "What oh-so-important visitor is here now?" she asked.
By the time Lila and Mama Anisa reached the village, a group of women was already standing around the visitor. Weary from their work-filled day, they listened in silence.
"...a plan to bring green back to this village," the visitor was saying.
Lila grabbed Mama Anisa's arm, but Mama Anisa's face was skeptical. "Perhaps she means well," Mama Anisa whispered, "but she may not know what she's talking about."
"So, Wangari Maathai, what is this plan exactly?" a woman asked, a baby in her arms. Her face looked as unbelieving as Mama Anisa's.
"It's simple," the visitor said. "We plant trees."
Now Mama Anisa grabbed Lila's arm. They listened as Wangari Maathai explained how trees protect the water and earth. "Who will join me?" she asked.
"Us?" someone asked. "Plant trees?"
"I have enough trouble growing a little food," another woman added.
"By the time the trees grow..." a third said, shaking her head.
"I'll help!" Lila cried. Everyone looked at her, but she didn't care.
"And I," said Mama Anisa. "It's a good plan."
Slowly, a few others raised their hands.
"Then it's decided," Wangari Maathai said. She looked straight at Lila. "Together, we women will bring back our green—and our blue."

title.text: The Day the Butterflies Were Found

passage.text: Rosa milked the cow, the milk splashing against the metal bucket. Nearby, Papá fed the donkey.
"Buenos días," a voice said.
Rosa glanced up to see a man and woman standing in the barn doorway. Outsiders, Rosa decided. She knew almost everyone who lived around here. Besides, the pair wore city clothes.
"Buenos días," Papá answered, standing up straight. "Can I help you?"
"Yes, thank you," the woman smiled. "I'm Catalina, and this is Ken. We're trying to find a secret place."
"A secret place?"
The man held up a picture of some orange-and-black butterflies. "Have you seen these butterflies?"
Papá laughed. "No secret there," he said. "They pass through every November."

"Hundreds of them!" Rosa added, coming to stand next to Papá. "Some say the butterflies are the spirits of our dead loved ones." Rosa wasn't sure what she thought about that. Still, she loved it when the butterflies came.
"They're beautiful, aren't they?" Catalina said. "Every winter, they fly away from Canada and the United States. But no one knows where they end up. It's like they just disappear!"

"The scientist we work for thinks they all live together someplace, maybe right here in Mexico," Ken said. "But Dr. Urquhart has been searching for years, and he hasn't found their spot yet. We're hoping to crack this mystery."
"Wow," said Rosa.

Papá pointed. "All I know is they head up the mountain." Then he frowned, thinking. "My uncle once spoke about a lovely, special place he'd found while gathering mushrooms. He said it was so spectacular that he thought he was in a dream. I wonder..."

Then Rosa remembered something. "Once when Grandmother and I were picking blackberries, she said our loved ones might be sleeping nearby. I thought she was just trying to stop my chattering. But maybe..."
"Do you remember where you picked the blackberries?" Catalina asked.
Rosa nodded.
"Perhaps we can help after all," Papá said.

An hour later, Rosa, Papá, Catalina, and Ken hiked up the mountain to the blackberry patch. They searched the whole area but saw no butterflies. Then, Papá bent down. "I think these are the mushrooms my uncle liked."
They followed the mushrooms to where they grew thickest. And that's when Rosa spotted a butterfly. "There!" she cried.
"Let's follow it!" said Catalina. The group pressed forward, winding around rocks and sliding down hills.
Suddenly, there was a sound like gentle rain. Everyone stopped and looked up. "Far out," Ken whispered.
The trees looked orange.
Their branches were covered with thousands, maybe millions, of butterflies! Rosa felt like she was in a beautiful dream. She stared until her neck ached.
"January 2, 1975," she whispered, knowing she'd never forget it.

header.text: Select the one preposition.

A preposition is a connecting word. It comes before a noun or pronoun and connects it to the rest of the sentence. The main noun or pronoun that comes after the preposition is called the object of the preposition.

sentences.text: I will call you after dinner.
The preposition is after. It connects the object, dinner, to the rest of the sentence.
